results.claim: The fixed-k problems are monotone under padding: k-Induced Disjoint Paths reduces to ℓ-Induced Disjoint Paths for every fixed ℓ≥k while preserving H3-freeness. Moreover, k=1 is linear-time solvable and every fixed-k problem is in NP.
results.proof_sketch: Given a k-pair instance, take its disjoint union with ℓ−k copies of K2 and designate each new edge as a terminal pair. This is a legal graph instance. Each added pair has exactly one connecting path, its isolated edge, and no original path can enter an added component. Hence restriction and extension give both directions of equivalence. Because H3 is connected and has eight vertices, a copy cannot span components and cannot lie in K2, so H3-freeness is preserved in both directions. For k=1, the terminals are linkable exactly when connected; a shortest connecting path is induced because any chord shortens it, giving O(n+m) time. For fixed k, the simple path sequences have polynomial size, and endpoints, edges, vertex-disjointness, chords, and inter-path adjacencies are polynomially checkable.

results.claim: Every H3-free graph is 6-degenerate, with the constant sharp; additionally, two vertices of degree at least three can never be at distance exactly three. Thus an n-vertex H3-free graph has at most 6n−21 edges for n≥7, and every connected H3-free graph of minimum degree at least three has diameter at most two.
results.proof_sketch:
Let u-x-y-v be a shortest three-edge path with deg(u),deg(v)≥3. Each endpoint has two neighbors besides its connector neighbor. Shortestness puts those four neighbors outside the connector, and the two endpoint-neighbor pairs are disjoint because a common member would give a u-v path of length two. The connector and four leaf edges therefore form H3 as a subgraph; extra edges do not matter. Thus such u,v cannot exist. The first and fourth vertices of any geodesic of length at least three yield the diameter consequence.

Every graph of minimum degree at least seven contains every eight-vertex tree: root the tree and embed it parent-first. When the jth vertex is embedded, its parent has at most j−2≤6 already used neighbors and therefore has an unused neighbor. Hence any subgraph of minimum degree seven contains H3, proving 6-degeneracy. In a degeneracy ordering, the first n−7 vertices contribute at most six forward edges and the final seven contribute at most 21, giving 6n−21. K7 is H3-free, has degeneracy six, and attains equality.

results.claim: H3-free graphs admit an arbitrary-routing-plus-matching normal form. Let R be any graph and M a matching on V(R), disjoint from E(R). Replace every edge of R by a four-edge path and retain every edge of M unsubdivided, obtaining G(R,M). Then G(R,M) is H3-free. With all terminals in V(R), induced linkages in G(R,M) correspond exactly to vertex-disjoint paths in R∪M such that every M-edge whose two endpoints are selected is itself used between consecutive vertices of one path. In particular, the H3-free class has unbounded treewidth.
results.proof_sketch:
Every subdivision vertex has degree two, so an H3 center must be original. Starting at an original vertex along an R-corridor takes four edges to reach another original. Starting along M reaches an original after one edge; since M is a matching, a simple path cannot then use a different M-edge, and two further corridor edges end at a subdivision vertex. Thus no three-edge path joins possible centers, so G(R,M) is H3-free.

A simple path with original endpoints that enters an R-corridor must traverse it completely: every internal corridor vertex has degree two. Contracting all such traversals therefore gives a simple path in R∪M, including the case where both corridor incidences belong to one path, and lifting reverses this operation. Distinct base paths lift to vertex-disjoint paths. An unused R-edge between selected originals causes no host adjacency because it was subdivided; the only possible chord or inter-path edge is an unsubdivided M-edge. It is harmless exactly when used consecutively within one path, proving the correspondence. With M empty and R=K_m, contracting the corridors gives a K_m minor, so treewidth is at least m−1 for unbounded m.

results.claim: For arbitrary graphs, hence also for H3-free graphs, k-Induced Disjoint Paths is fixed-parameter tractable in k+b, where b is the number of vertices of degree at least three. There is an exact equivalent compression with at most b+binom(b,2)+6k vertices.
results.proof_sketch:
Let B be the b vertices of degree at least three. Every component of G−B is a path, isolated vertex, or cycle and has at most two attachment edges. A terminal-free component can occur in a simple terminal path only as a corridor between two distinct B vertices. Dead ends and components attached twice to the same B vertex would force termination at a nonterminal or repetition; parallel corridors with the same distinct endpoints are interchangeable, so retain one two-edge representative per unordered pair.

For each terminal-bearing component, order its terminals and B-attachment occurrences along the path or cycle; the same B vertex may occur at both ends. Discard terminal-free tails. Between consecutive marked occurrences, retain a one-edge gap exactly and replace every longer gap by a two-edge path. Internal gap vertices have degree two and are not terminals, so a solution either avoids a gap or traverses it completely; expansion and contraction preserve simplicity, inducedness, disjointness, and all cross-path edges. A detached cycle with exactly one terminal is immediately NO; cycles with at least two terminals are handled cyclically.

There are at most b+2k marked vertices, at most binom(b,2) generic corridor representatives, and at most 4k gap representatives: a path component with t≥1 terminals has at most t+1≤2t gaps, while a cycle has t. Thus the bound is b+binom(b,2)+6k. Exhaustive enumeration on the compressed graph is a function of b+k, and construction and certificate lifting are polynomial.

results.claim: A globally shortest path for one terminal pair cannot be fixed greedily, even on a seven-vertex H3-free graph.
results.proof_sketch: Use vertices s1,t1,x,s2,t2,y,z and edges s1x, xt1, xs2, s2t2, s1y, yz, zt1. The graph is H3-free because it has only seven vertices. Exact simple-path enumeration gives s1-x-t1 as the unique length-two, hence globally shortest, s1-t1 path. Every s2-t2 path contains s2, and xs2 is an edge, so no induced linkage can contain that shortest path. Conversely, the simple induced paths s1-y-z-t1 and s2-t2 are vertex-disjoint and have no edge between them. Thus replacing one member of a solution by a globally shortest path is not a valid greedy rule.

final_writeup:
This remains a partial result. It does not classify the problem for any fixed k≥2, so the requested all-k complexity classification is not solved.

For k=1, the problem is in linear time: connectivity is sufficient because every shortest connecting path is induced. Padding by isolated K2 components gives exact reductions from k to every fixed ℓ≥k, so future hardness propagates upward and an algorithm for ℓ propagates downward. Every fixed-k problem is also in NP.

H3-freeness supplies real but insufficient structure. Such graphs are sharply 6-degenerate, have at most 6n−21 edges for n≥7, and cannot contain degree-at-least-three vertices at distance exactly three. In particular, connected H3-free graphs of minimum degree at least three have diameter at most two. These facts do not imply bounded treewidth: replacing every edge of K_m by a four-edge path produces an H3-free graph with a K_m minor.

More generally, four-edge subdivisions of an arbitrary routing graph may be augmented by an unsubdivided matching. Induced linkages then project exactly to vertex-disjoint paths in the routing graph plus matching, subject to one explicit conflict rule: whenever both endpoints of a matching edge are selected, that edge must be used consecutively by one path. This construction identifies a possible hardness framework, but it is not itself a hardness proof because matching edges are traversable rather than merely forbidden.

On the algorithmic side, if b is the number of vertices of degree at least three, every instance has an equivalent kernel-like compression with at most b+binom(b,2)+6k vertices. Consequently the problem is FPT in k+b. This does not settle the target because H3-free graphs can have unbounded b; for example, K3,n is H3-free and has unboundedly many degree-at-least-three vertices.

Finally, the seven-vertex example proves that even when a solution exists, fixing a globally shortest path for one pair can destroy all solutions. Thus the most direct greedy approach fails.

The unresolved task for each fixed k≥2 is therefore still to exploit stronger H3-free structure on an unbounded branching set, or to establish hardness while controlling the traversable matching conflicts in the subdivision construction. Claimed resolution: PARTIAL.
